prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Court May Consider Documents Incorporated by Reference in the Complaint Without Converting the Motion to Dismiss into One for Summary Judgment.**

Rule 12(d) requires conversion to summary judgment when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). The Ninth Circuit has long held that documents incorporated by reference into a complaint are not "outside the pleadings" for this purpose. A court "may . . . consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003). Defendant's motion relies on documents of this kind, and the Court may consider them.

**A. The incorporation-by-reference doctrine is settled in this Circuit.**

The doctrine is old. A court may consider "documents whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party questions, but which are not physically attached to the [plaintiff's] pleading." *Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002). The Ninth Circuit has repeatedly reaffirmed this rule. *See Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006) (applying the rule to a document not attached to the complaint whose authenticity was undisputed).

The doctrine reflects the principle that a plaintiff cannot avoid dismissal by omitting from the complaint the document on which the claim is based. *See Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). The doctrine "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). It is a "judicially created doctrine that treats certain documents as though they are part of the complaint itself." *Id.*

**B. The documents at issue satisfy the doctrine's requirements.**

A document is incorporated by reference "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 907–08. Either ground is enough. *See id.*; *Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010). The doctrine also applies where the plaintiff's claim depends on a document's contents, the defendant attaches the document to its motion, and no party questions its authenticity. This holds even if the complaint does not expressly quote the document. *Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076; *see also In re NVIDIA Corp. Sec. Litig.*, 768 F.3d 1046, 1058 n.10 (9th Cir. 2014) (considering documents incorporated by reference in the complaint).

Each requirement is met here. The Complaint refers to the documents and relies on them as the basis for its claims. [Insert record citations, e.g., Compl. ¶¶ __.] Defendant has submitted true copies of them. [Insert declaration citation.] Plaintiff cannot reasonably dispute their authenticity, because Plaintiff's own allegations depend on them. Considering them therefore does not convert the motion. *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.

**C. Considering the documents does not require the Court to resolve factual disputes.**

Defendant asks the Court to consider what the documents say. It does not ask the Court to accept Defendant's account of disputed facts. The Ninth Circuit distinguishes between these two uses. A court may consider a document's contents once it is incorporated, but it "may not . . . take judicial notice of disputed facts" and should not assume the truth of a document's contents when they are reasonably disputed. *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 999–1003; *see Lee v. City of Los Angeles*, 250 F.3d 668, 688–89 (9th Cir. 2001). Defendant relies on the documents only for what they say. They contradict, or fail to support, the Complaint's characterizations of them. Where a complaint's allegations are contradicted by a document it incorporates, the Court need not accept the allegations as true. *See Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002–03; *Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A.*, 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012) (considering a document that formed the basis of the plaintiff's claim).

**D. Conclusion.**

The documents are incorporated by reference. The Court may consider them under Rule 12(b)(6) without converting the motion under Rule 12(d), and it should do so in deciding the motion.
